lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: The most common way to understand probability, and the one most of us meet first, is to see it as a frequency.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: In this view, when you say the chance of heads is one half, you are saying that if you flipped this coin many, many times, the share of heads would settle closer and closer to one half.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: Flip it ten times, and you might well get seven heads.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: Flip it a hundred times, and the share is already closer.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: Flip it a million times, and it is practically glued to fifty percent.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: People have actually done this, by hand.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: In the eighteenth century, the naturalist Buffon flipped a coin four thousand and forty times, and got two thousand and forty-eight heads.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: The statistician Karl Pearson flipped twenty-four thousand times, and got twelve thousand and twelve.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: And during the Second World War, a mathematician named John Kerrich, held in an internment camp in Denmark, flipped ten thousand times, and got five thousand and sixty-seven heads.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: Every one of them, a hair away from one half.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: This is the law of large numbers, first proved by Jacob Bernoulli in a book published in seventeen thirteen.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: It says that the frequency you observe will converge to the theoretical value as the number of trials grows.

lines.section: The world that runs on frequencies
lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: This way of seeing things is enormously useful, and a huge number of systems around us are built on it.

lines.section: The world that runs on frequencies
lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: A casino makes money not because it cares who wins this round, but because it cares about millions of rounds.

lines.section: The world that runs on frequencies
lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: An insurance company doesn't need to know whether you will have an accident. It needs to know how many, out of a million customers, will.

lines.section: The world that runs on frequencies
lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: A factory checking the quality of its products works by the very same logic.

lines.section: The world that runs on frequencies
lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: The key thing in all these examples is that they can be repeated.

lines.section: The world that runs on frequencies
lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: You can keep flipping the coin, keep making new batches, keep selling new insurance policies.

lines.section: The world that runs on frequencies
lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: That repeatability turns a frequency into a number you can measure and test, so any argument can be settled with real data.

lines.section: The world that runs on frequencies
lines.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
lines.text: For problems of this kind, the frequency view is almost the natural choice. The trouble lies with the problems that are not of this kind.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: Try applying the frequency view to sentences like these.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: The probability that it rains in Hanoi tomorrow is seventy percent.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: The probability that a new drug passes its phase three trial is thirty percent.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: The probability that this candidate wins the election is sixty percent.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: There is only one tomorrow, and it will not repeat.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: That drug is tested only once, in exactly the way it is being tested.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: That election happens exactly once in history. There are no million tomorrows for you to count how many were rainy.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: People who hold the frequency view have a rather clever answer for the weather.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: They say the seventy percent is not about tomorrow at all. It is about the whole collection of days on which the forecast said seventy percent.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: If, among all those days, roughly seven in ten really did turn out rainy, the forecast is called well calibrated.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: It is a lovely idea, and it is exactly how forecasting models are scored in practice.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: But that answer cannot rescue every case.

lines.section: Back to the coin under my hand
lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: Go back to the coin lying under my hand. It has already landed. There is no collection to put it in.

lines.section: Back to the coin under my hand
lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: The event has happened, and the result is fixed.

lines.section: Back to the coin under my hand
lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: And this is the point where I feel I need to stop and think a little harder.

lines.section: Back to the coin under my hand
lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: Suppose I sneak a look at the coin, and you don't.

lines.section: Back to the coin under my hand
lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: For me, the probability is now one hundred percent, or zero. For you, it is still fifty.

lines.section: Back to the coin under my hand
lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: The coin did not change at all in the instant I looked. Only the information changed.

lines.section: Back to the coin under my hand
lines.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
lines.text: And that small observation leads straight to the second way of understanding probability.

lines.section: A property of you, not of the coin
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: The second view says that probability measures how strongly you believe a statement, given the information you have.

lines.section: A property of you, not of the coin
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: In this view, probability is a property of the relationship between you and the event. It doesn't live inside the coin, or the cloud, or the ballot.

lines.section: A property of you, not of the coin
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: It describes the state of your knowledge.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: At first this sounds far too loose, as if anyone could believe whatever they like.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: But in fact it is tightly constrained.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: In the nineteen twenties and thirties, Frank Ramsey in England and Bruno de Finetti in Italy, working independently, showed that if you want your beliefs to be consistent, they are forced to obey exactly the rules of probability.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Their argument is built on betting.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Suppose you are willing to bet according to exactly how strongly you believe things.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Now suppose your numbers break the rules. In a match with only two possible outcomes, you believe team A will win with seventy percent, and at the same time you believe team B will win with fifty percent.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Then someone can sell you two tickets. One pays a dollar if A wins, and by your own belief it is worth seventy cents. The other pays a dollar if B wins, and by your own belief it is worth fifty cents.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Each ticket looks perfectly fair to you, so you buy both, for a dollar twenty.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: But exactly one team will win, so you will collect exactly one dollar. Whatever happens, you lose twenty cents.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: So the rules of probability don't fall from the sky. They are the conditions for your beliefs not to contradict themselves.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: What I love about this view is that it handles events that happen only once.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: You can perfectly well talk about how strongly you believe that Mars once had life, even though that is simply true or false, and will never be repeated.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Once probability is a belief, a new question appears. When new information arrives, how much should you change your mind?

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Bayes' theorem answers that question. Let me walk through a concrete situation, so it is easy to picture.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: A text message pops up on your phone, claiming to be from your bank.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: The hypothesis you are weighing is this. The message is a scam.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Until now, messages from this number have almost always been genuine, so your starting belief leans heavily towards genuine.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Picture it as a pair of scales, tipped deep to one side.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: The message opens with "Dear valued customer". So you ask yourself two questions.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: First, if this is a scam, how likely is it to open so politely? Quite likely.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Second, if this is genuine, how likely is it to open exactly like that? Also quite likely.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: The ratio between those two answers is the weight of the evidence.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Here the two numbers are almost equal, so the ratio is close to one. Multiply the scales by it, and they barely move.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: You have read the greeting, and you have really learned nothing.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: You read on, and the message asks you to reply with your one-time password.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: If it is a scam, that request makes perfect sense. If it is really your bank, it almost never happens.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: Now the two numbers are far apart, the weight is large, and the scales swing hard.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: That is the heart of Bayes' theorem.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: A piece of evidence is convincing not because it fits your hypothesis, but because it would be unlikely if your hypothesis were wrong.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: A sign that shows up about equally often whether the hypothesis is true or false tells you almost nothing, however impressive it looks.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: And one more thing. The scales only shift. They are never reset from scratch.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: If you start from a hypothesis that is extremely unlikely, with the scales tipped very deep, a single piece of evidence is usually not enough to pull them back to the middle.

lines.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales
lines.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
lines.text: That sounds obvious. But in the next part I will show you just how easily it gets forgotten.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: Here is a classic example from medicine.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: Suppose there is a disease that affects one person in every thousand. And there is a test for it.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: If you really have the disease, the test comes back positive ninety-nine percent of the time.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: If you are perfectly healthy, there is still a five percent chance it comes back positive by mistake.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: You take the test, and it comes back positive. What do you think is the chance that you really have the disease?

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: The easiest way to see it is to count real people.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: Imagine one hundred thousand people all taking the test.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: About one hundred of them really have the disease, and the test catches ninety-nine of them.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: That leaves ninety-nine thousand nine hundred healthy people. With a five percent false alarm rate, about four thousand nine hundred and ninety-five of them get a positive result too.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: So in total, about five thousand and ninety-four people are holding a positive result. And only ninety-nine of them are actually sick.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: Ninety-nine out of five thousand and ninety-four, is about two percent.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: In other words, even with a positive result in your hand, the chance that you are really ill is only about two percent.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: That number surprises a lot of people, and not only beginners.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: In nineteen seventy-eight, researchers at Harvard put almost exactly this question to sixty doctors, residents and medical students. Nearly half of them answered ninety-five percent.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: The reason is that most of us focus on how accurate the test is, and forget how rare the disease was to begin with.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: That starting rate matters enormously, yet it slips out of view without a sound.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: When a disease is rare, the healthy people are so numerous that just a few percent of false alarms is enough to swamp the people who are truly sick.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: And notice what made it easy. Counting people, instead of juggling percentages.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: Psychologists call these natural frequencies, and simply rewriting the problem this way makes far more people get it right.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: Counting, the frequency view, turns out to be the best tool for updating a belief.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts
lines.text: The lesson of this example is that the same test result can mean very different things, depending on the background information you start from.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: By now you might think these two views are two rival schools of mathematics. In fact, they are not.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: In nineteen thirty-three, Andrey Kolmogorov put probability on a rigorous mathematical foundation, built on just three axioms, and they are surprisingly simple.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: He said that a probability is a rule that gives every event a number, such that, first, no value is ever negative.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: Second, the certain event gets the value one.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: And third, for events that are mutually exclusive, meaning they can't happen together, the probability that one of them happens is the sum of their separate probabilities.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: That is all.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: The whole of modern probability theory is built on those three conditions.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: And what is remarkable is that nowhere in those three axioms is there a single line saying what probability means.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: Kolmogorov gives you the rules of the game, not its meaning.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: Seen from mathematics, a probability is just a measure, from the same family as the way we measure area and volume, with the convention that the whole space of outcomes has measure one.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: When you say an event has probability three tenths, you are saying it takes up three tenths of that space.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: The frequency view and the belief view both satisfy these axioms.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: That is why the two sides can argue fiercely about meaning, and still share the very same set of tools for calculation.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides
lines.text: Frequentists and Bayesians build different statistical methods, and answer different questions. But neither of them is doing the mathematics wrong.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: There is a deeper question, and to me it is the most fascinating question in this whole video.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: A coin flying through the air is a physical object obeying Newton's mechanics.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: If you knew exactly the force of the flick, the angle, the spin, the height, and the way the hand catches it, you could calculate the result. There is nothing mysterious in it at all.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: Persi Diaconis, a mathematician who was once a professional magician, showed this in a very practical way.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: He and his colleagues built a coin-tossing machine with fixed settings, and it gave the same face every single time.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: His team also showed that a coin flipped by hand and caught in the palm is slightly biased towards the face that started on top, about fifty-one percent of the time.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: In twenty twenty-three, a team of researchers tested this with more than three hundred and fifty thousand real flips, and found fifty point eight percent. Almost exactly what the theory predicted.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: So if you had seen which face was up when I flicked my coin at the start of this video, your number would not be fifty percent. It would be fifty-one.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: The coin is the same coin. Once again, only the information changed.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: So the randomness of a coin is not inside the coin.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: It lies in the fact that the result is extremely sensitive to starting conditions that our hands cannot control, and our eyes cannot measure.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: Randomness, here, is another name for missing information.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: With the weather, with markets, with traffic, the story is much the same. They are complicated, and extremely sensitive to where they start, but they are not mystical.

lines.section: The one place the story isn't settled
lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: To be fair, there is one place where this story is not settled.

lines.section: The one place the story isn't settled
lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: Down at the scale of single particles, quantum mechanics behaves very differently.

lines.section: The one place the story isn't settled
lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: Experiments built on a result called Bell's theorem, which earned the Nobel Prize in Physics in twenty twenty-two, have ruled out the idea that each outcome is simply written in advance, in hidden information the particles carry with them.

lines.section: The one place the story isn't settled
lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: Whether that is true randomness, or something stranger still, physicists are still debating.

lines.section: The one place the story isn't settled
lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: But a coin is not an electron. For the coin, the weather and almost everything in our daily lives, the uncertainty lives in us.

lines.section: The distance between you and the coin
lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: So, in the end, probability is often introduced as a tool for talking about how random the world is.

lines.section: The distance between you and the coin
lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: But look closely, and it is a disciplined way of writing down what you don't yet know.

lines.section: The distance between you and the coin
lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: The fifty percent at the start of this video says nothing about the coin. It describes the distance between you, and the coin.

lines.section: The distance between you and the coin
lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: Thank you for watching all the way to the end.

lines.section: The distance between you and the coin
lines.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
lines.text: If this changed the way you hear the word probability, subscribe to ninety-nine percent from scratch, so you don't miss the next one. See you soon.
